1. Genealogies after H. Djajadiningrat, ‘Critisch overzicht van de in Maleische werken vervatte gegevens
over de geschiedenis van het Soeltanaat van Atjeh’ (BKI 1911); Encyclopaedie van Nederlandsch Oost-
Indie, art. ‘Atjeh’, Vol. 1 (1917); and H.M. Zainuddin, Tarich Atjeh dan Nusantara 1 (Medan 1961).
2. There are great differences between traditional chronicular accounts and contemporary evidence
(epigraphy, European reports). The oldest Aceh rulers according to the former are as follows: Johan Syah
1205-35, S. Ahmad or Ri’ayat Syah 1235-57 (son), N.N. 1257-98 (son), Raja Mahmud or S. Firman Syah
1298-1344 (son), Raja Mansur Syah or Alauddin Johan Syah 1344-98, Raja Mahmud 1398-1456 (son), S.
Husain Syah 1456-90 (son), S. Ali Ri’ayat Syah 1496-1511, S. Salahuddin Syah 1511-29 (No. 5. in the
above table) etc. Epigraphical data record the existence of Sultan Suleiman bin Abdullah bin al-Basir (dead
1211) who ruled Lambri/Lamuri, a predecessor of Aceh.
3. The genealogical positions of the queens 18.-20. are uncertain. That No. 19. was the daughter of No. 18.
is stated in a few chronicles, but unknown to contemporary materials. According to a local genealogy in
Banda Aceh, No. 18. Nur al-Alam was the daughter of Raja Mahmud Radhiah, son of No. 14. Ali Ri’ayat
Syah. According to the same source, No. 19. Inayat Syah was the daughter of Mahmud Syah, son of
Sulaiman Syah, son of Abdul Jalal, son of No. 6. Alauddin Ri’ayat Syah. And further, No. 20. Kamalat
Syah would have been the daughter of Raja Umar, son of Muhyuddin, son of No. 9. Sri Alam.
 4. A manuscript preserved at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur, gives the following pedigree
for the queens; see A. Hasjmy, 59 tahun Aceh merdeka dibawah pemerintahan ratu (Jakarta 1977).

zelfbesturende landschappen in de Residentie Timor en Onderhoorigheden’ (Indische Gids 1925 & 1934);

3. The genealogy of Jacob Ch. Amabi is considerably longer than the one constructed here: Neno – Salolo
(No. 4. above) – Balas (No. 8.) – Baltasar (No. 9.) – Muni – Kusa – Lelo – Nobe – Neno – Afu (No. 12.) –

(Saroro Neno) is succeeded by his sons Balbesi and Balthazar, and the genealogy then runs: Balthazar (No.
9.) – Slolo (No. 11?) – Osu I (No. 10?) – Osu II (No. 14.) – Nobe – Mano (No. 15.). Also, in the
Middelkoop version No. 17. Kusa is the first cousin, not the second cousin, of No. 16. Lelo.
4. A traditional account mentions Bi Osu, daughter of Mano, as ruler after No. 17. The matter would require
further investigation.

Commentary:
1. Genealogy after traditional and Dutch texts in Coll. C.C. Berg 118, Leiden; R. Friederich, ‘Voorloopig
verslag over het eiland Bali’ (VBG 1849-50); and H. Schulte Nordholt, Macht, mensen en middelen (M.A.
thesis 1980). There are several differences between indigenous family trees and Dutch accounts.
2. Friederich has the following early genealogy: 1. G. Ngurah Bola - 2. Anak Agung Ketut Mandesa - 3.
Anak Agung Padedekan - 4. G. Nyoman Tegeh [G. Jambe Pule] - 5. G. Ngurah Jambe Mihik [Merik] - 6.
Anak Agung Telas ring Batu Krotok - 7. G. Ngurah Sakti Pamecutan [No. 5 in the above list] etc. The list
here follows the indigenous babad texts.
3. Ruler No. 6, Den Pasar line, is omitted by Friederich, who makes No. 7 the son of No. 5.
34

4. Ruler No. 7, Pamecutan line, is omitted by Friederich, who makes No. 8 the son of No. 6.
5. No. 10 of Pamecutan line is not counted as ruler by the babad texts, who presents No. 11 as successor of
No. 9. It has been considered proper here to follow the European accounts.
6. Some babads have an extra generation, Gusti Gede Ngurah Pamecutan, in the succession of Den Pasar
kings, between ruler No. 9 and the titular king Gusti Ngurah Made. Again, the witness of European reports
has been followed here.
7. Dutch reports mention an unnamed king of Kuta, brother-in-law of the Gelgel king, in 1633, further a
Radja Tiou (Raja Cau) of Badung in 1666, a Gusti Agung Badung in 1692, and a Gusti Panjatsjoetan
(Pamecutan) in 1704. A document of 1768 mentions four kings in the Badung area: Gusti Moera Jambij,
Gusti Cajanan, Gusti Panatjoetan and Gusti Moera Non, and a letter from 1783 two: Gusty Moera
Cayangang and Gusty Moera Calerang.
8. The death of No. 10 of the Den Pasar line is sometimes placed at 1863, which is however contradicted by
contemporary Dutch evidence.

Commentary:
1. After A. Rasyid Asba et al., Silsilah kekerabatan Raja-Raja Sulawesi Selatan-Barat (Jakarta 2015); H.
Saharuddin, Mengenal Pitu Babana Binanga (Mandar) dalam lintasan sejarah pemerintahan daerah di
Sulawesi Selatan (Ujung Pandang 1985); local genealogy; and Memorie van overgave - Afdeeling Mandar
(1940) in Coll. Leyds, H 1153:17, KITLV.
2. The pedigree of forefathers of the Balangnipa royal line is according to tradition as follows: Tamatau -
Diangmemang - Makkediang - Puangditeko Banuanna - Batara Lattu - Batara Lumiling - Batara Tukka -
Batara Tau - Puang ri Bate - Puang di Mamasa - Puang di Bola - Kadaru Bulabang - Tama Lelengang -
Liaulangi - Sulu Alle - Paderang - Pongkopadang - Simba Datu - Tabittueng* - Todiurraurra - Weapas* -
Todilaling [No. 1 above], etc.
3. Tomatindo di Pamaisang, wife of No. 15. is sometimes stated to have been ruler rather than her husband.
4. A ruler called Daeng Mabani is recorded in 1672. Later a ruler called Daeng Rioso (No. 12.) was
deposed on 23.11.1680, and succeeded again by Daeng Mabani. Furthermore, a Daeng Burane was deposed
by the Pambauang ruler Mangindano Daeng Tulolo in the 1690s but restored in 1699. A Satuburou was
king of Mandar in 1712. Their identity with any persons in the above genealogy is not clear.

1. Genealogy after S.O. Robson, ‘The Ancient Capital of Bali’ (Archipel 16 1978); Sejarah Nasional
Indonesia II (Jakarta 1993); H. Creese, ‘Balinese Babad as Historical Sources’ (BKI 147 1991); and I.W.
Warna et al., Babad Dalem (1986). The indigenous dates after 1500 are found in Babad Gumi (LOr
10.548), Babad Bhumi (Coll. V.E. Korn Or. 435, KITLV) and Wariga (LOr 3662).
2. The reign of No. 23. is traditionally put in the age of Gajah Mada (14th century) while No. 25. would
have survived the fall of Majapahit (about the 1520s), providing an impossible chronology.
3. The chronology of the later Bali kings (No. 23.-32.) is subject to much controversy and uncertainty. In
one view (H. Creese), No. 27. ruled in the 1630s, No. 28. died in c.1650 and No. 29. ruled c.1655-65. See
also H. Hägerdal, Candrasangkala: The Balinese Art of Dating Events, online resource, http://lnu.diva-
portal.org/smash/get/diva2:206791/FULLTEXT01.pdf
4. The first king of Klungkung, Dewa Agung Jambe (from 1686) is traditionally though doubtfully
represented as son of No. 29.

Commentary:
1. In main after genealogy in Ministerie van Kolonien, Politieke verslagen buitengewesten 1924/26, Fiche
706, NA; and A.C. Kruyt, ‘De vorsten van Banggai’ (Koloniaal Tijdschrift 1932); and J.J. Doormeier,
‘Geschiedkundige aanteekeningen betreffende Banggai en Gapi’ (BKI 102 1943). See also Sejarah Daerah
Sulawesi Tengah (Jakarta 1979). Some of the dates from Pusat dokumentasi kerajaan2 di Indonesia,
Vlaardingen.
2. A traditional list of rulers before the instigation of the Banten dynasty runs as follows: 1. Gahani-
Gahanii; 2. Tahani-Tahanii; 3. Adi Kalut Pokalut; 4. Adi Moute; 5. Adi Lambal; 6. Mumbu Pakalalos doi
Tano; 7. Mumbu Pakalolos doi Ndalangon; 8. Mumbu Palangkangkang; 9. Mumbu Tetelengan; 10.-12.
Unknown kings 13. Mumbu Aibinggi.
3. Contemporary Dutch sources mention a Daeng Bolikang as governor for Makassar from 1664, a Kabudo
in or before c.1680, Jangkal until 1680, Kalkebulang from 1680, Sammutsiu as jogugu from 1682,
Kubukubulang in 1689, Kalsum (or Kitjil Kasim) in 1741-49, and Kitjil Sitoer Molucco from 1749. While
some of these may be tentatively identified with persons in the traditional genealogy, others remain
unknown.

Commentary:
1. The first Buleleng dynasty after P. Worsley, Babad Buleleng; A Balinese Dynastic Genealogy (‘s-
Gravenhage 1972); U.P. Tisna, Pahlawan nasional Patih Jelantik: seorang Ksatria Buleleng (Jakarta
1996); genealogy in Coll. V.E. Korn Or. 435:211, KITLV; and excerpts from Dutch 17th and 18th century
sources in Coll. H.J. de Graaf, H 1055:8, KITLV. The Karangasem dynasty after genealogies in Coll C.C.
Berg 118, Leiden.
2. The death of No. 1. is stated to be c.1704 by H. Schulte Nordholt (Een Balische dynastie, Ph.D. thesis,
Amsterdam 1988), though Dutch texts seem to place it earlier, between 1697 and 1699.
3. Certain genealogies seem to indicate that Gusti Wayan Padang, son of No. 1., and his two sons, are no
more than duplicates of No. 2. and his two sons.
4. The Babad Buleleng differs from contemporary sources by calling No. 2. G. Ngurah Panji Gede, and by
letting the latter be succeeded by G. Ngurah Panji Bali, son of his brother G. Ngurah Panji Made. Panji Bali
is then depicted as father of 4a. and 4b. We follow here Dutch sources in combination with a genealogy
reproduced by P.L. van Bloemen Waanders, ‘Bijdragen tot de kennis van het eiland Bali’ (TNI 3:2 1868).
5. Van Bloemen Waanders lets No. 4b. be succeeded by his son G. Made Jelantik and grandson G. Made
Singaraja, though the story of their co-rule is a duplicate of what is told about 4a. and 4b. in the Babad
Buleleng and the Babad Kramas (LOr 15.014). All this would require further investigation.

3. An alternative list of liurais of Fatuaruin runs as follows: Suku Lorok, Tei Ekin [i.e. No. 4.?], Kfau
Funan, Sasila Mean [ i.e. No. 8], Tei Beran [i.e. Tei Seran, No. 9]. The two lists are thus at considerable
variance, demanding further investigation.
4. An oral account, by Dominikus Tei Seran [14.], asserts that No. [12] Ulu Bau Taen was the uncle, not
nephew, of No. [11.] Fatin Tei Seran. The pedigree from the 1960s asserts that Edmundus Tei Seran was the
grandnephew of No. 13 Luis Terek Seran, which seems to present chronological difficulties.
5. European sources mention a number of rulers of Belu who can not be associated with the names of the
traditional lists. Dom Caethano da Costa was “king of the province of Belu” in 1731-32, and a female
Liulai [Liurai] was ruler in 1732. Jacinto Correia was the grand prince of Belu and raja of Wewiku-Wehali
in 1756-57, and António de Melo was raja of Wehali in 1767. No. 6 Don Alesu Fernandes is attested from
an inscription on a tongkat and governed in 1769 without being legitimate king. One liurai Nai Tey reigned
in 1855 and died in 1858. According to one source the liurai-ship was vacant for more than 30 years until at
least 1889. Still a source asserts that a liurai called Dominggus (usually identified as Manek Mesak) died in
c. 1890, and his widow Teli Seran ruled in place of their son Na’i Kin, born c. 1880.

resemblance to contemporary data; see I. Taniputera, Kerajaan-kerajaan Nusantara pascakeruntuhan

Ledalmasu – Etu Ledak – Bebe Etu – Solu Bebe – Li Solu – Poi Li – Tua Poi – Tamulu Tua – Telema

– Bulu Bole – Koli Bulu – Leo Koli – Ndeo Leo [No. 6.?] – Angi Ndeo – Leuana Angi (see above), etc.

traditional genealogies have several variants, and the pedigree is not stabilized and anchored historically
until the mid 19th century.

names have been left out. A ruler in late 16th century, Prabu Landak, is said to have left as his heir a

(1608-22). For the 18th century, Malay chronicles mention a number of names not found in the above list:

Ratu Bagus seems to be the son of No. 15 in the above table which does not, however, point him out as a
raja. For the variants, see P.J. Veth, Borneo’s Weesterafdeeling (Zaltbommel 1854-56); the Hikayat Upu
Daeng Menambon, in F. Schulte, Die Chroniken von Sambas und Mempawah (Heidelberg 1991); and Raja
Ali al-Haji, Tuhfat al-Nafis. For the main genealogy given here, see H 43, KITLV; J.F. Later, Memorie van
Overgave van de Onderafdeeling Landak (1919), KIT 981, NA; Ministerie van Kolonien, Politieke
verslagen buitengewesten (1898), Fiche 393, ARA; Coll. A.H. Boehm, No. 22, NA; and local Landak
genealogy.
2. Some lists insert a ruler Pangeran Bupati Kesuma Sari between No:s 8. and 12. Others omit altogether
the generation between 8. and 12.
3. Ya’ Unus Pangeran Temenggung, the father of the regent Panembahan Gusti Muhammad Tebri, Pangeran
Wiranata (1883-90), is alleged in alocal source to have acted as regent between Nos. 11 and 13. There is no
trace of him in Dutch sources, however.
4. After the murder of the last regular ruler Abdul Hamid, Gusti Affendi acted as a regent from 25.3.1946
until jailed by the Dutch on 22.10.1946. From 21.1.1947, there was a zelfbestuur committy, consisting of
Urai Johan, Temenggung Penes and Temenggung Dawat. See Rapportage Indonesie 1945-1950, No. 587,
NA.

ceased to exist in c.1518 or c.1527, though little can be said with confidence.

Commentary:
1. Mainly after L.Y. Andaya, The kingdom of Johore 1641-1728 (Kuala Lumpur 1975); C. Dobbin, Islamic
Revivalism in a Changong Peasant Economy: Central Sumatra, 1784-1847 (London and Malmö 1983);
Generale Missiven; and J. Drakard, A Kingdom of Words: Language and Power in Sumatra (Selangor
1999). As the royal court at Pagaruyung was destroyed in about 1815, there exists little materials for a
reconstruction of the royal genealogy, and the above names are mostly taken from external, European,
sources. The kingship was traditionally divided in three lines, first between a main king and two
Bendaharas as co-regents, and later between Raja Alam, Raja Adat and Raja Ibadat, the division stemming
from a throne crisis after 1674. Raja Alam of Pagaruyung was the highest titularis.
2. No. 9b. gives his pedigree as the son of S. Abdullah Syah, son of S. Alauddin Syah, son of S. Abdul Jalil
Syah, brother of S. Malfar Syah, son of S. Mahmud Syah, son of S. Ahmad Syah, son of S. Mansur Syah,
son of S. Malfar Syah. The identity of these with otherwise documented persons is somewhat hypothetical.
3. About 1600, a Datu Mahkota, who preached Islam in South Sulawesi, is said to have been “Sultan of
Pagaruyung” – an unlikely claim.
4. An Abdul Jalil is mentioned as an important ancestral figure in several sources; he may be identified on
one hand with a Minangkabau prince called Abdul Jalil who displayed political activity in 1740-43, and on
the other hand with a Sultan Abdul Jalil Muazzam Syah mentioned in royal seals as the grandfather of a
later ruler; besides, current Minangkabau tradition mentions a ruler Abdul Jalil or Muningsyah as the father
of the founder prince Rala Malewar of Negri Sembilan in Malaysia (fl.1728-47), and grandfather of the last
precolonial ruler 11b. Whether these various references to Abdul Jalil refer to one and the same individual
is a moot point since Abdul Jalil can also be interpreted as an emblematic prestige name.
5. No. 11a. had a young son who became Sultan in Pagaruyung in c.1759, maybe the same as No. 12a.
6. There are various legendary Minangkabau rulers mentioned in the literature. They are traditionally
counted as descendants of Iskandar Dzulkarnain (Alexander the Great). An indigenous account in ‘Abstract

2. The early dates (before 1800) are taken from the work of A. Rachman et al. and cannot be corroborated
from external materials; from Western and Malay sources it is only known that a certain Saboa Tangan
Pangeran ay de Paty Sambas (Raja Tengah, father of 2.?) ruled in 1609, and that ruler No. 4. flourished in
c.1720 and No. 6. in 1792 and 1794.
3. The names of the rulers in the chronicle used by De Hollander differ from those of other sources. Thus
No. 1. is called Ratu Pisseban, No. 2. Sultan Muhyuddin, No. 3. Sultan Jalaluddin, No. 4. Sultan
Muhammad Jalaluddin, No. 5. Sultan Abu Bakar Kamaluddin, No. 6. Sultan Omar Akamuddin, No. 7.
Sultan Abu Bakar Tajuddin, No. 8. Sultan Muhammad Ali Safiuddin, No. 9. Sultan Usman Kamaluddin,
and No. 10. Sultan Omar Jalaluddin.
4. After the murder of No. 15., no more sultans were installed. In the time of the West Borneo pseudo state,
from 1946, Pangeran Temenggung Jayakusuma filled the role of chairman of the                      zelfbestuurcommissie
under the auspices of the Dutch.

Commentary:
1. Genealogy of the main Sonba’i branch after P. Middelkoop, ‘Iets over Sonba’i’ (TBG 1938); L.J. van
Dijk, ‘De zelfbesturende landschappen in de Residentie Timor en Onderhoorigheden’ (Indische Gids 1925
and 1934); Hans Hägerdal, Lords of the Land, Lords of the Sea: Conflict and Adaptation in Early Colonial
Timor, 1600-1800 (Leiden 2012); Ch. Th. Weidner, Nota van toelichting betreffende het landschap Mollo
(1932), KIT 1289, NA; Timor papers of the VOC, in NA, The Hague; Timor papers of ANRI, Jakarta; F.H.
Fobia, Sonba’i (unpublished manuscript 1984); and unpublished genealogy dated 1954.
2. For the rulers 5.-16., European sources have been used, in particular the Generale Missiven; P.J. Veth,
‘Het eiland Timor’ (De Gids 1855); and the Timor missives of the VOC at Nationaal Archief, The Hague.
The names of rulers 1.-6. are so far only known from traditional genealogies.
3. There are several variations between different traditions as to the exact pedigree of the Sonba’is. In
particular, there is disagreement whether Baob Sonba’i was the son of Neno Sonba’i or Talus Sonba’i.
4. According to the Timorese traditions, the Sonba’i Kecil line split off from the main liurai line shortly
before (or, in another version, after) the Dutch arrived to West Timor, establishing themselves close to
Kupang. In Dutch documents the bulk of the Sonba’i population arrived to Kupang area in September
1658, continuing to enthrone “emperors” and acting regents (No. 1.-18. in the above genealogy). The
remaining inland Sonba’i submitted to the Dutch in 1749. A merger between the two Sonba’i groups was
effected shortly 1776, but from 1782 the main liurais came to rule at Kauniki, while the other branch, the
Sonba’i Kecil, were still in charge in westernmost Timor. Genealogy of the latter line from P.F.J. Kortleven,
Memorie van Overgave van de afgetreden Resident van Timor en Onderhoorigheden (1931) [KIT 343,
NA]; and the Timor papers at the NA, The Hague. For traditional accounts see G. Heymering,’Bijdragen tot
de geschiedenis van Timor’ (TNI 9:3 1847); and S. Müller, Reizen en onderzoekingen in den Indischen
Archipel (WKI II 1857).
5. The succession in the period 1821-39 is obscure. According to S. Müller a Sonba’i Kecil emperor passed
away some years before 1828, and was succeeded by a grandson. Perhaps the grandfather is No. 9. and the
grandson is No. 12. in the above table but this is no more than conjecture. An Ote alias Pieter Aulasi is
mentioned as ruler in Sonba’i Kecil in 1832; he should be No. 12. According to the Memorie of Kortleven
he ruled between No. 14. and No. 15., but in the Dutch official reports there is no trace of him in the 1870s.

Commentary:
1. List mostly after P.J. Veth, Borneo’s Westerafdeeling 1-2 (Zaltbommel 1854-56); J.U. Lontaan, Sejarah-
hukum adat dan adat istiadat Kalimantan Barat (Jakarta 1975); H. von Dewall, ‘Matan, Simpang,
Soekadana, de Karimata-eilanden en Koeboe’ (TBG 11 1862); J.B.J. Barth, ‘Overzicht der Afdeeling
Soekadana’ (VBG 50 1896); and Coll. A.H. Boehm, No. 22, NA. There are some differences between the
various traditional accounts, and when comparing these with contemporary sources.
2. Ruler No. 9 is called Radin Wiera Cassoema in contemporary Dutch sources. A Pangeran Putra is known
from the 1630s and 1640s, and a second Wiera Cassoema in the 1640s, though their precise positions are
unclear.
3. Certain Malay chronicles, as Tuhfat al-Nafis, have No. 12. and No. 13. as sons of No. 11.
4. Late tradition identifies Raden Saradewa with ruler No. 11., which seems to be contradicted by older
chronicles. Also, modern tradition makes No. 11. the son-in-law rather than son of No. 9. and 10.
5. The dates before the late 18th century are mostly conjectural and uncertain. According to traditions
recorded by G. Muller (in P.J. Veth 1854-56), No. 11. ruled 1624-77, the two regents 1677-94, No. 12.
1677/94-1725 and 1727-32, No. 13. 1725-27, and No. 14. 1732-36. Modern tradition has No. 11. rule 1622-
59 and No. 12. 1659-1717 or 1728, which might be closer to the truth. Judging from Malay chronicles,
especially Tuhfat al-Nafis, No. 13. was deposed about or before 1720 and No. 15. flourished in 1749.
6. Some lists have No. 19. as the son of one Pangeran Ira Nata, cousin of No. 18. This Ira Nata would have
been the son of Pg. Cakra (Pg. Agung), of a branch of outcasts, requiring further investigation. Barth (1897)
has both versions. We follow here the genealogy given by P.J. Veth.
7. After the murder of the last ruler Panembahan Saunan, there was a regency council consisting of Uti
Halil alias Pangeran Mangku Negara, Uti Aplah alias Pangeran Adipati, and Uti Kencana alias Anom
Laksamana. In the West Borneo pseudo-state, Uti Aplah served as waarnemend zelfbestuurder under Dutch
auspices.
8. The exact ties between the Simpang and Matan lines are not clear from the material; according to H. von
Dewall (TBG 11 1862), Kusumaningrat of Simpang was the son of a Pangeran Adipati, son of No. 12.,
while tradition recorded by G. Muller (in P.J. Veth) gives the above genealogy.
9. Gusti Lekar of Meliau is mentioned as son of No. 9. rather than of No. 1. in the Silsilah Melayu dan
Bugis, which fits better with the Meliau-Tayan genealogies.

Commentary:
1. Taken from J. Noorduyn, Bima en Sumbawa (VKI 129 1988); Lalu Manca, Sumbawa pada masa lalu
(Surabaya 1984); H. Hägerdal, Held’s History of Sumbawa (Amsterdam 2017); and W.G. van der Wolk,
Memorie Soembawa (1941), H 1087, KITLV. There are several differences between the two former texts as
regards the regnal list.
2. Lalu Manca makes No. 8. rule to 1760, followed by Datu Ungkap Sermin 1761-62 and then No. 10.
1762-65. He further calls No. 11. “Mahmud”, asserting that Mappaconga Mustafa was the name of a regent
during the period 1765-1776.
3. The period 1816-37 was filled by two non-royal regents: Nenerang  Mele Manyurang (1816-1820 or
1825) and Mele Abdullah (1825-36).
4. Sumbawan traditions are not very explicit, so that much of its history must be reconstructed from
external sources. Tradition as reported by Lalu Manca (1984) mentions Dewa Lengit ling Baremang, Dewa
Lengit ling Kartasari, and Dewa Maja Paruwa, as rulers before No. 1. above. However, Dewa Maja Paruwa
is also (in the Bima chronicle, Or. 506 (a), KITLV) represented as father of the princesses Mas Surabaya
and Mas Panghulu, who according to contemporary sources were daughters of a Selaparang king.
According to Van der Wolk, the first ruler mentioned by local accounts is a Datu Sampar Samulan (Dewa
Won Kuning), succeeded by Datu Poro, under whom Islam was introduced (1618); then follow Datu Apitai
(No. 4. in the above list), Mahmud (No. 5.), Datu Loloh (No. 6. in the above list), Kaharuddin (No. 14.),
Amrullah (No. 16.) etc. Thus, there are a lot of black holes and contradictions in the local tradition.

Commentary:
1. After S. Hayase et al., Silsilahs/Tarsilahs [Genealogies] and Historical Narratives in Sarangani Bay and
Davao Gulf Regions, South Mindanao, Philippines, and Sangihe-Talaud Islands, North Sulawesi, Indonesia
(Kyoto 1999); Generale Missiven; local genealogy by the raja family; and information provided by Pusat
Dokumentasi Kerajaan2 Indonesia, Vlaardingen.
2. For parts of Tahuna’s history, the precise dynastic information is sparse. This is in particular so with the
Rasubala dynasty. According to certain data a H. Rasubala would have ruled in 1716-36, who is
unmentioned by contemporary sources. Also, one list has Zacharias Dirk Rasubala and Paneke as one
single ruler. Alternative dates are given for some rajas: Zacharias Dirk Rasubala Peneke 1779-1800,
Tabaleta Rasubala 1800-20, Jacob Rasubala Saraweta 1820-41, Egenos Laurens Tamarol 1841-58, Walanda
Jacob Rasubala 1858-70, A.T. Rasubala Limampulo 1870-75, Egenos Laurens Tanaru Rasubala 1878-87.
These dates may be spurious.
3. In the contracts written between the Dutch colonial government and the various rulers, the names are
sometimes given differently. Thus the ruler in 1828 would be called Albertus Jacobus Jacobsz, and the
successor of Marten Jacobsz after 1875 is called either A.T. Rasubala Limampulo or Egenos Lorens
Tamarol (or Tanaru) Rasubala.
4. Tahuna and Kendahe were proclaimed to be united into one rajaship in 1893, though this became
effective only from 1903.

to the main rulers of the region. It has not been possible to include all the petty rajas in the above table.

were later by convenience included under this geographical name.

1. In the absence of indigenous records, the first part of the genealogy (until 1657) draws upon various
Iberian and Dutch sources, in particular Leonardo de Argensola and the documents collected by H. Jacobs
(Documenta Malucensia 1-3, Rome 1974-84). See also f.i. P.A. Tiele, ‘Der Europeers in den Maleischen
Archipel’ (BKI 25-36 1877-87); P.J.B.C. Robidé van der Aa, Reizen naar Nederlandsch Nieuw-Guinea ('s-
Gravenhage 1879); and Ch. van Fraassen, Ternate, de Molukken en de Indonesische Archipel (Ph.D.
Thesis, Leiden 1987). The second part is mainly taken from a genealogy in Coll. Coolhaas, NA. 20th
century data after Memories van Overgave, NA; and an unpublished local genealogy. The regnal dates
mostly after E. Katoppo, Nuku (Jakarta 1984).


355

2. The list of early rulers is traditionally given as follows: 1. Sah Jati, 2. Busamuangi, 3. Suhu, 4.
Balibungah, 5. Duhu Madoya, 6. Kie Matiti, 7. Sele, 8. Matagena, 9. Ciri Leliatu (Jamaluddin), 10. Mansur,
11. Amiruddin Iskandar Dulkarnain, 12. Kie Mansur, 13. Iskandar Sani, 14. Gapi Baguna Sirajul Arafin, 15.
Mole Majimu, etc. See F.S.A. de Clercq, Bijdragen tot de kennis der Residentie Ternate (Leiden 1890). The
genealogical details for most of them are no longer remembered by tradition; No. 8. Matagena might have
begun a new dynasty in the 15th century.
3. A sultan called “Bungua”  is known in 1564 and 1570. Bungua could also be a mutilated form of Gapi
Baguna.
4. The Coolhaas genealogy makes No. 12. Syaifuddin the son of a Sultan Saiduddin (No. 11. Saidi), son of
Sultan Alauddin (No. 9. Ngarolamo). We follow here the contemporary European records.
5. No. 15 Hasanuddin is represented as the son of his predecessor Mansur in the Coolhaas genealogy and in
Katoppo. Contemporary European evidence, however, contradicts this.
6. Katoppo makes No. 17. the son of No. 16. The Coolhaas genealogy has been followed here.
7. Katoppo further states that No. 20. was the son of No. 17. Again, the Coolhaas genealogy has been
deemed the most trustworthy source.
